preamble: Fortition of the palatal lateral [ʎ] to the voiced palatal stop [ɟ], with the lateral approximant closing completely at the palatal place. The clearest case is Sicilian: Latin /lj/ first yielded a geminate palatal lateral [ʎʎ] throughout Southern and Central Italy (still heard in Italian figlio, aglio), and in Sicilian this [ʎʎ] appears as geminate [ɟɟ], spelled -gghi-: figghiu 'son', ogghiu 'oil', agghiu 'garlic'. Central-southern Sicilian (Agrigento, Caltanissetta, Enna) further weakens -ggh- to the fricative [ʝ]. The Spanish example formerly filed here was a chain: yeísmo merged /ʎ/ into /ʝ/, and [ɟ] is a positional allophone of /ʝ/, so it is not a direct ʎ > ɟ shift.

examples.note: The geminate palatal lateral from Latin -LJ- surfaces as a geminate voiced palatal stop.
